clue.text: Carrot or stick in prospect?

parts.note: to stick or jam is to become wedged fast
something in prospect lies ahead, coming the next day

explanation.surface: A political question: is voters' reward or punishment what lies ahead?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carrot or stick' reads as one stock phrase, but 'Carrot' alone is the definition and 'stick' starts the wordplay. The phrase comes from Alice Through the Looking-Glass: jam yesterday, jam tomorrow, but never jam today.
explanation.definitionFit: A carrot is an enticement, and the idiom names a pleasant reward that is promised but never actually delivered.

clue.text: Quite an attack on staff in decline — more likely outcome of 1A

parts.note: quite in the sense of exactly or precisely, as in 'just right'
a bout is a spell or attack, as of illness
to man a post is to staff it
ageing (US spelling) means growing old, in decline

explanation.surface: A grumble that something is quite an attack on workers in decline, likely the result of promises left unkept.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase was Theresa May's label for struggling families, abbreviated JAM, which ties it to the jam promised at 1 Across.
explanation.definitionFit: Those fed only promised rewards end up barely coping, scraping by with little to spare: the likelier result of empty pledges.

clue.text: See 1
Weighs down on youngsters saving nothing

parts.note: on can mean over, as a book on or over a subject

indicators.note: saving means keeping something safe inside, so one word holds the other within it

parts.note: lads are young boys
nothing is zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: Someone puts heavy pressure on young people who can't put a penny aside.
explanation.definitionFit: To burden with too much is to weigh down, with the verb in the same present-tense form.

clue.text: Bad! Starts to attack old person's telly not being freely available

indicators.note: bad means in a poor or disordered state, so the letters are jumbled
starts to the following words means only their opening letters are taken

explanation.surface: A complaint that an older viewer's television is under assault, no longer free to watch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starts to' takes the first letters of attack, old, person's, telly, not (AOPTN), and 'Bad' signals that they are rearranged. 'being' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Beer drawn straight from the barrel is always ready to serve, so the idiom describes anything readily obtainable.

clue.text: Resistance to pressure in one school or another

parts.note: R is the symbol for electrical resistance

indicators.note: in places one item inside the other

parts.note: Eton is one famous English public school
P is the symbol for pressure

explanation.surface: Resistance to pressure is found in one school or another, as if about peer pressure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one school' gives ETON, so 'or another' is left as the definition: another such school. ETON and Repton are both English fee-paying boarding schools.
explanation.definitionFit: Repton is a Derbyshire boarding school, so it is another school beside the first one named.

clue.text: Old German is to join up

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the letters are read from the bottom, backwards

parts.note: to sew is to join with stitches

explanation.surface: An elderly German is going to stitch things together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' signals reversal because this is a down entry, read from the bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: Wessi was the informal term for a citizen of the former West Germany, a state that no longer exists, hence old.

clue.text: Braved elements defiantly, perhaps

indicators.note: elements are component parts, so the word's letters are taken apart and rebuilt

explanation.surface: Someone faced the weather with defiance, perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Braved elements' reads as facing bad weather; here 'elements' tells you to rearrange the letters of 'Braved'.
explanation.definitionFit: Defiantly is a word modifying a verb, an example of that part of speech, which 'perhaps' signals.

clue.text: Worry lover's dropped note

indicators.note: dropped means let go, so those letters fall away from the word

parts.note: a lover can be a kept woman; the 's stands for has
mi is a note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A worried partner has lost a note, perhaps a love letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Anxiety or strain is a source of worry, so the two nouns name the same troubled state.

clue.text: Finds it difficult to keep city clean

indicators.note: to keep is to hold, so one set of letters keeps the other inside it
difficult means awkward or troublesome, so the letters are put in disorder

parts.note: EC is the postcode for the City of London

explanation.surface: Someone struggles to keep a town tidy.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of 'Finds it', rearranged by 'difficult', hold EC, from 'to keep'.
explanation.definitionFit: To sanitise by killing germs is to clean thoroughly, a verb in the same form.

clue.text: It is opportunity to hold back advance

indicators.note: back means the hidden letters are read in reverse
to hold is to contain, so the answer sits within these clue words

explanation.surface: A chance to hold someone back from progressing.
explanation.walkthrough: TISOP sits inside 'It is opportunity' ('hold'), and 'back' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: To put forward an idea or argument is to advance it as a premise, a verb in the same form.

clue.text: Gospel in centre of church rejected by setter

indicators.note: rejected means thrown back, so the word is reversed

parts.note: the nave is the central body of a church
gel is something that sets, as hair gel does

explanation.surface: Sacred teaching is spurned at the heart of a church by the puzzle setter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'setter' looks like the crossword compiler but is GEL, something that sets.
explanation.definitionFit: This is an old word for the good news of Christ's teaching, a synonym of the noun.

clue.text: See 17
British have cause to rebel? It might be OK

parts.note: to own is to have

indicators.note: to rebel is to rise up against order, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: The British have a cause for revolt, and perhaps that's all right.
explanation.walkthrough: OK is a British brand of fruity sauce, so 'OK' is not 'all right'. The answer also nods to Gordon Brown, matching the theme of political pledges.
explanation.definitionFit: OK Sauce is a branded variety of the dark condiment, so it is an example of the definition.

clue.text: Woman with children to Romeo is a fool to return

parts.note: Romeo is R in the NATO phonetic alphabet

indicators.note: return means go back, so these letters are read backwards

parts.note: a nit is a fool

explanation.surface: A woman with children by a lover is a fool to go back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'return' reverses A NIT to make TINA.
explanation.definitionFit: Christina is a female given name, so it is an example of a woman.

clue.text: See 22
Consumer goods Ben briefly carried in helicopter to US

indicators.note: carried means held within, so these letters go inside the other word

parts.note: an eater is a consumer of food
G is good, and GG is the plural, goods

indicators.note: briefly means cut short, so the last letter goes

explanation.surface: Shopping for Ben is flown briefly by helicopter to America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'briefly' cuts BEN to BE; GG and BE are 'carried in' EATER.
explanation.definitionFit: In American slang a helicopter's whirling rotor recalls a kitchen whisk, so the name became slang for the aircraft.

clue.text: Con or lie — it seems largely designed to gain power

definitions.text: Con or lie — it seems largely designed to gain power

indicators.note: to gain is to take on, so the letters take in the next one
designed means arranged to a plan, so the letters are rearranged
largely means most of it, so the last letter is cut

parts.note: P is the symbol for power

explanation.surface: A cynical view of political pledges: cons or lies designed to win office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'largely' cuts SEEMS to SEEM; CONORLIEITSEEM is rearranged ('designed') and gains P ('to gain').
explanation.definitionFit: A pledge made to voters during a campaign is, in the cynic's view, a deception designed to win office.

clue.text: Regularly spin tosh as Parliament does

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so alternate letters are taken

explanation.surface: A dig at politicians who keep spinning rubbish, as Parliament does.
explanation.definitionFit: A parliament holds its sessions when in session, and the verb matches the clue's 'does'.

clue.text: Glossy container put in as an illustration

indicators.note: put in means placed inside another word

parts.note: say introduces an example, as an illustration
a tin is a container

explanation.surface: A shiny container is placed as a showpiece.
explanation.definitionFit: Having a smooth sheen like the fabric means lustrous, so the adjective is a synonym.

clue.text: Grant for one when time's right (no longer without news)

parts.note: as means when, as in 'as I left'
T stands for time; the 's means has

indicators.note: without means lacking, so those letters are taken out

parts.note: news is read as N's, two letters N

explanation.surface: A grant comes when the time is right, though no longer without news.
explanation.walkthrough: 'news' is read as N's: removing both Ns from 'no longer' leaves OLOGER.
explanation.definitionFit: Russell Grant is a British TV stargazer known for horoscopes, so he is an example of one.

clue.text: Stay on team

parts.note: re means on or concerning
a side is a team

explanation.surface: A manager tells a player to stay in the team.
explanation.definitionFit: To live or dwell somewhere is to stay there, a verb in the same form.

clue.text: Listen to Labour — it's showy but worthless

indicators.note: to labour is to work over, so the letters are worked into new order

explanation.surface: A jibe that the Labour Party's message is all glitter and no substance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Labour' looks like the party but tells you to rearrange 'Listen'.
explanation.definitionFit: Used as an adjective, the word describes cheap glittery decoration: gaudy and of little value.

clue.text: Quite content one's charged following dip in river — for which 26 said sorry

indicators.note: to dip in is to go into, so the letters go inside the river

parts.note: the Tees is a river in north-east England

indicators.note: content means the contents, so the inside letters are taken

parts.note: an ion is a charged atom

explanation.surface: Someone is quite happy to pay after a swim in the river, but someone apologised for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 26 is NICKS: Nick Clegg, as Liberal Democrat leader, broke a pledge on university charges and later said sorry for it.
explanation.definitionFit: Students' university charges in England rose in 2010 despite a Liberal Democrat pledge, for which their leader Nick Clegg publicly apologised.

clue.text: Old people's home about to shut — basic accommodation lacking

parts.note: in means at home
ca is short for circa, about

indicators.note: lacking means without, so those letters are removed

parts.note: a hut is basic accommodation

explanation.surface: An old people's home is about to close for lack of basic accommodation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old people's home' reads as a care home, but 's is 'has' and 'home' gives IN.
explanation.definitionFit: These were the ancient Andean civilisation of Peru, a people of the past.

clue.text: Studs — they're slow to get topless

indicators.note: topless means the top or first letter is removed

parts.note: garden molluscs famous for slowness

explanation.surface: Studs are slow to get their shirts off.
explanation.definitionFit: Small metal fastenings with heads, like studs, are a synonym, as in hobnails.

clue.text: Report helps those conned

indicators.note: report means a spoken account, so the word is as heard

parts.note: succours means helps or aids

explanation.surface: A report helps people who have been swindled.
explanation.definitionFit: Dupes or easy marks are people who have been tricked, a plural noun.

clue.text: Recalled Charlie in coat and trousers

indicators.note: recalled means called back, so the letters run backwards
in places one letter inside the word

parts.note: a skin is a coat, as on fruit or animals
Charlie is C in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Charlie is recalled to the shop in a coat and trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trousers' is a verb: to pocket, steal.
explanation.definitionFit: Both verbs mean to steal or pocket, slang synonyms for taking without paying.

clue.text: Hold back, it's assumed, after one started

indicators.note: after places the rest behind the first letter

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: assumed means taken on, so the letters are taken inside
back means read in reverse

parts.note: to detain is to hold
it, with 's meaning is

explanation.surface: Someone holds back, it is assumed, having started first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hold back' gives NIATED; 'assumed' takes IT inside; 'after one' puts I first.
explanation.definitionFit: To set something in motion is to begin it, so the past form means begun.

clue.text: Point wrong near start of manifesto — liars, it's a work of fiction!

parts.note: S, south, is a compass point

indicators.note: wrong means not right, so the letters are put out of order
start of means the first letter is taken

explanation.surface: A wrong point in a manifesto exposes liars: the whole thing is fiction!
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrong' looks like it describes the point, but it is the signal to rearrange; 'it's' is a link before the definition, George Eliot's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: George Eliot's 1861 novel about a reclusive weaver is a celebrated piece of fiction.
